trivia: Maria is by far my most common name: almost 900,000 people carry it, about one in every 31 residents. The most common man's name is António, with around half a million, followed closely by João.

trivia: I am one of the youngest countries on Earth. Half of my roughly 39 million people are under about 17, and women here have around five children on average.

The first Africans recorded in the English colony of Virginia, in August 1619, were my people. Captured in wars in my old kingdom of Ndongo, they were on a slave ship bound for Mexico when English privateers seized them.

trivia: Kizomba, the slow, close partner dance now taught in studios from Lisbon to Paris, was born in Luanda in the late 1970s and 1980s. Its name comes from the Kimbundu word for 'party'.
My high-energy street dance and music, whose name means 'hard bottom', was born in the late 1980s. Some of its jerky, limping moves were inspired by people who lost limbs to landmines during the war.
Samakaka, my bold wax-print cloth, is full of old geometric symbols. In its classic colours, black stands for Africa, red for the blood of the liberation struggle and yellow for the country's wealth.
In my southern highlands, Mwila women coat their thick braids in oncula, a red paste of crushed stone. The number of braids carries meaning: wearing three signals a death in the family.

trivia: My capital, Luanda, is the most populous Portuguese-speaking capital city in the world, bigger than Lisbon and Brasília.
About 71% of my people speak the old colonial language, but nearly a quarter speak Umbundu, my most widely spoken African language, from the central highlands.

trivia: Every 11 November I celebrate independence from Portugal, proclaimed in 1975. Civil war broke out almost immediately and lasted, on and off, until 2002.
My National Heroes' Day, 17 September, is the birthday of my first president, who was also a doctor and my most celebrated poet. His face is on my banknotes.
My national dish, muamba de galinha, is chicken stewed in red palm oil with okra and hot gindungo chilli. It's eaten with funge, a stiff cassava porridge you pull off by hand to scoop up the sauce.
My basketball team, nicknamed after a rare black antelope, is Africa's most successful: 12 AfroBasket titles, including six in a row from 1999 to 2009 and a 70–43 final win at home in 2025.

trivia: In my Namib desert grows Welwitschia mirabilis, a plant with only two leaves that keep growing for its whole life, which can be well over 1,000 years. It survives by drinking the sea fog.
My national symbol is a rare antelope with huge curved horns, found nowhere else. After 27 years of war it was feared extinct, until camera traps photographed a herd in 2005.

trivia: Kalandula Falls drops 105 metres along a horseshoe 400 metres wide, making it one of the largest waterfalls in Africa by volume.
One of my provinces is cut off from the rest of me by a 60 km strip of a neighbouring country. That small piece of me produces about 60% of my oil.

trivia: Near one of my highland cities, the plateau ends at a rim more than 2,200 metres high and then drops about 1,000 metres straight down, with views over 10,000 km² of lowlands.
Miradouro da Lua, the 'Viewpoint of the Moon', about 40 km south of Luanda, is my most visited attraction: ochre cliffs carved by wind and rain into lunar-looking pinnacles above the Atlantic.
My first UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 2017, is a small northern plateau town. It was the capital of one of Africa's great kingdoms from before the Portuguese arrived in 1483 until 1915.
reveal: Mbanza Kongo, capital of the Kingdom of Kongo

trivia: When a Portuguese governor offered her no chair, Queen Njinga had a servant kneel on all fours and sat on them, so she could negotiate eye to eye. She fought the Portuguese for decades.

trivia: In 1987–88, around a small town in my southeast, my army and Cuban troops fought South African forces in the biggest conventional battle on the African continent since the Second World War.

In January 1997 the world's most famous woman put on a visor and body armour and walked through a live minefield in my second city. Her visit helped push the world towards a landmine ban; the minefield is now a busy street with a school named after her.

trivia: In 2017 Luanda was ranked the most expensive city in the world for expatriates, ahead of Hong Kong, Tokyo and Zurich.
As Africa's second-largest oil producer, pumping about 1.1 million barrels a day, I walked out of OPEC in January 2024 after 16 years, rather than accept a cut to my production quota.
In December 2024 I received the first-ever visit by a sitting US president, who came to see a 1,300 km railway being rebuilt to carry copper and other minerals from inland Africa to my Atlantic port.

trivia: A Chinese state company built me a whole new city of 750 eight-storey apartment blocks in about three years, for $3.5 billion paid back in oil. With flats at $120,000 or more, the world called it a ghost town in 2012.

trivia: I am one of the world's top ten diamond producers. In 2022 a riverbed mine of mine produced a 170-carat pink diamond, the largest pink found in 300 years; the same mine had already yielded a 404-carat white stone.

Visitors take home carved replicas of O Pensador, 'The Thinker', a Chokwe figure of a wise elder holding his head. The original was found in a diviner's basket in 1932, and it became a national symbol in 1984.
